reason: Not an equivalence claim: the mutant is observable and killed by ChunkedDecoderTests.testFeedReturnsWhenBodyBufferIsEmpty, hand-verified (RED under the mutant: an XCTestExpectation times out after 2.0s waiting for feed(_:) to return; GREEN restored: passes in well under a second). The mutant makes the .body case's early return unreachable when the buffer is already empty, so feed(_:) spins forever re-processing a zero-byte take instead of returning - a genuine infinite loop, not merely a slow test. Reported Timeout directly in every file-scoped tool run taken for this bead (both before and after the fix), so no tool run - the tool always runs the whole test target, it has no per-test scope - can report this mutant Killed within its 120s budget.

Unreachable branch. This is the else of the receive handler's four-way branch (lines 47-55): it runs only when NWConnection reports no content, no error and isComplete false. Over a stream connection asked for minimumIncompleteLength 1 that combination does not occur - no content always arrives with isComplete or an error, both handled above. Probed with 250 receives (200 racing close(), 50 racing peer EOF, plus receives after EOF and before open): every one reported bytes, isComplete, or a transport error, never empty content, so no test can reach the deleted statement.

Proven equivalent. isFinished is read in one place, the guard at line 142, whose other clause is resultBeforeAttach == nil. Line 132 runs only on the path where resultBeforeAttach is non-nil (line 127), and nothing ever sets it back to nil, so that clause alone refuses every later finish whether this assignment writes true or false. attach runs once per gate, so there is no other reader.

Proven equivalent. The unlock at line 133 is the last use of that gate's lock. Reaching line 133 means resultBeforeAttach was set, which only happens in finish when no continuation is attached (line 147) - that is the cancellation handler at line 104, which runs at most once. attach then returns false and perform returns without calling operation(gate) (lines 100-101), so the NWConnection call that would produce further finish calls never starts. Nothing acquires the lock again; the mutant only leaves an NSLock locked when it is deallocated, which reports nothing. The whole suite passes clean with this mutant applied.

Proven equivalent. perform reads this return only to decide whether to start the operation (lines 100-101). On this path the continuation has already been resumed with the result that arrived before attach, and the gate is settled - line 132 sets isFinished and resultBeforeAttach stays non-nil - so line 142 refuses every later result and an operation started here can no longer reach the caller. That result can only have come from the cancellation handler, which cancels the connection immediately after producing it (lines 104-105), so the operation the mutant starts runs on a cancelled NWConnection and performs no I/O. SocketConnectionTests.testACallStartedInACancelledTaskNeverDialsThePeer pins that: with this mutant applied the peer still accepts no connection.

Proven equivalent. Line 143 runs only on a gate that is already settled, and nothing acquires that gate's lock afterwards in any sequence a caller can produce: attach runs once and before the operation starts, the cancellation handler runs at most once, and the open state handler - the only source of repeated finish calls - settles a gate and then sees only .cancelled, handled at line 84. The mutant therefore leaves an NSLock locked when it is deallocated, which reports nothing; a further finish on that dead gate could only block a callback of a connection that has already been cancelled, with no result left to deliver either way. The whole suite passes clean, in 13s, with this mutant applied.

Proven equivalent. finish's return value is read in one place, the open state handler's if gate.finish(...) at line 80, which runs only for .waiting and .failed. Reaching line 144 there needs the gate to be settled already, and neither way of settling it leaves a second .waiting or .failed to arrive: the first one settles the gate and cancels the connection (lines 80-81), after which the connection reports only .cancelled, handled at line 84 where the result is discarded; and a connection that reached .ready over a Unix socket reports the peer's exit to the pending receive as EOF or an error, not as a state change. The extra connection.cancel() this mutant would cause is unreachable.

Proven equivalent. finish's return value is read in one place, the open state handler's if gate.finish(...) at line 80. Line 149 returns from the branch where no continuation is attached, which needs finish to run before attach - that is the cancellation handler at line 104, whose result is discarded. For the state handler's own gate the continuation is always installed first: perform calls operation(gate), which assigns the handler (line 26), only after attach returned true (lines 100-101). A later finish on that gate is refused at line 142 and returns from line 144, not 149.

Proven equivalent. With isFinished left false the settled gate still cannot resume twice: self.continuation is set to nil on the same path (line 152), so a later finish takes the guard let continuation else branch and stores its result instead of resuming. What the mutant changes is that later finish's return value - true from line 149 instead of false from line 144 - and the only reader of that value is the open state handler at line 80, which cannot reach it: settling a gate there cancels the connection (lines 80-81), after which only .cancelled arrives (line 84, result discarded), and a connection that reached .ready over a Unix socket reports the peer's exit to the pending receive rather than as a .waiting or .failed state change.

Proven equivalent, because of the close on the next line. The reader task suspends in exactly three places, all of them SocketConnection calls - open (line 44), send (line 45) and the receive inside pumpFrames (line 99); everything between them is synchronous, and AsyncThrowingStream.yield never suspends. connection.close() at line 40 cancels the NWConnection, and a cancelled connection ends every one of those calls: SocketConnectionTests.testSendFailsOnceTheConnectionIsClosed, testReceiveFailsOnceTheConnectionIsClosed and testAFailedOpenLeavesNothingDialling pin that. So the reader stops whether or not it was cancelled first. What the cancel changes is which error the reader ends with, and the stream has already terminated by then - its termination handler is what is running - so that error goes to a continuation that discards it. EventStreamTests.testDroppingTheStreamHangsUpOnTheDaemon and testTheClientHangsUpWhenTheDaemonEndsTheStream cover the two ways the stream ends and pass with this statement deleted; the statement stays because stopping the reader on its own terms rather than through a socket error is the right shape, not because a test can tell the two apart.

Not an equivalence claim: the mutant is observable, but no run that observes it can finish. hold() returns still holding the lock, so every later cancel() on that handle blocks its caller for good - including an event stream's termination handler, which runs on whichever thread dropped the stream, the main one included. Run on its own, PendingTaskTests.testCancelDoesNotWaitForTheTasksCancellationHandler fails on its 2s deadline under this mutant (measured: 'Executed 2 tests, with 1 failure (0 unexpected) in 2.111 seconds'). Run as the suite, the first dropped event stream parks the thread that dropped it and the suite never reaches its end (measured: killed at 250s, still inside ClientLoggingSitesTests). A run that never ends is scored Timeout before any output is read, so no test can have this mutant reported killed.

Proven equivalent. This is takeTheServiceDown's return value on the path where registrar.stopAgent() succeeds; its only reader is runServiceVerb's `if isServiceUp, press == servicePresses { start() }`. On this path record(.stopped) has already run (line 433), setting intent to .stopped before the return is read, and start()'s own guard requires intent == .running (line 117) - so calling start() with the mutant's isServiceUp=true is a guarded no-op. The only way intent could be .running again by the time isServiceUp is read is a later Start press, but that increments servicePresses first (runServiceVerb's own press/queued bookkeeping), which fails `press == servicePresses` and skips the start() call entirely before intent even matters. No sequence of calls can make the mutant's true reach an unguarded start().

No scoped tool run can report that, because this guard is what every call to start() passes through, and start() is what most of ThrowntomClientTests dials through - directly or via connectedClient()/StubStateTransport-style helpers. Breaking it fails every one of those tests' own bounded waits (each ~5s), and the full ThrowntomClientTests target does not finish inside the tool's 120s budget: measured, with this exact mutation hand-applied, `swift test --filter ThrowntomClientTests` ran 346 tests with 104 failures in 257.746s. A report that never finishes is scored Timeout before any test outcome is read, so no tool run - scoped by file, by operator, or otherwise, since the tool has no per-test scope - can report this mutant Killed.

Not an equivalence claim: this mutation produces source semantically identical to the guard's `intent == .running` NegateConditional mutant at 117:11 (`!(intent == .running)` and `intent != .running` are De Morgan-equivalent for this Equatable comparison, not byte-identical text), so it fails the same way for the same reason and is killed by the same hand-verified test, DaemonClientTests.testStartDialsTheEventStreamWhenIntentIsRunning. It reported Timeout directly even in a run with every NegateConditional mutator disabled (`--disable-mutator NegateConditional`, /tmp/report-ThrowntomClient-noNegate.json), confirming it is not merely poisoned by a neighbor but genuinely blocks the full suite past the tool's 120s budget on its own, for the mechanism recorded at 117:11's entry above.

Proven equivalent. omittingEmptySubsequences only controls whether zero-length components of the split are present in the result. payload(of:)'s loop immediately does `guard line.starts(with: dataPrefix) else { continue }` (SSEFrameSplitter.swift:55), and dataPrefix is 5 bytes ("data:"), so a zero-length line can never satisfy it -- it is skipped whether or not it appears in the split result. No frame's payload can differ between the two settings.

Proven equivalent. lf's match starts with 0x0A ("

") and crlf's match starts with 0x0D ("

"); the same byte cannot begin both, so l.lowerBound == c.lowerBound is unreachable and `<=` picks the same branch as `<` in every case this switch can actually reach (l.lowerBound < c.lowerBound picks l either way; l.lowerBound > c.lowerBound picks c either way).

Not an equivalence claim: the mutant is a real, deterministic, fast trap -- every existing ReconnectBackoffTests test constructs a backoff with a positive registerEvery, and precondition(registerEvery < 0, ...) then fails on the very first construction. Hand-verified: `swift test --filter ReconnectBackoffTests` with this mutation applied by hand aborts the whole process (`Precondition failed: the agent has to be registered at some point`, ReconnectBackoff.swift:18, exit via signal 5) before any test result is read; restored, the same filter passes 7/7. The tool can only ever score a process abort as Crash, never Killed, for a mutant of this shape -- there is no way for it to report a clean pass/fail from inside an aborted process. Not the file+operator-sharing SIGKILL-poisoning pattern docs/decisions/swift-mutation-timeout-poisons-a-later-mutant.md describes and the dispatch forbids excluding this way: there is no Timeout mutant anywhere in this file's own gated set to have poisoned it.

Proven equivalent for every input a test can safely construct. `registerEvery > 0` and `registerEvery >= 0` agree for every value ReconnectBackoff is ever constructed with in real use (all positive) and for every negative value (both trap). The only value where they disagree is registerEvery == 0, and probing it crashes the correct, unmutated code too -- precondition failures are not catchable in Swift -- so no XCTest can pass while observing that boundary; a test written to try would abort under the original implementation exactly as it is supposed to. There is no input for which a test can observe original and mutant behaving differently.
